guide.title: Bath Beach, Brooklyn: The Beach Under the Shore Parkway
guide.intro: Bath Beach, named for the English spa of Bath, Somerset, was developed as a recreational seaside retreat for affluent families. It was part of the original Brooklyn town of New Utrecht, and although Coney Island was nearby, Bath Beach also had its own amusement park. The population grew at the end of 1863, when steam dummy railroad service connected the community to the City of Brooklyn horsecar terminal at 25th Street and 5th Avenue in Sunset Park. It held one of Brooklyn's earliest African-American settlements: freed people were given a parcel of land here in the mid-nineteenth century, and the church that community formed, Mount Zion Baptist, later moved to Bedford-Stuyvesant. In the early 1900s many Italian immigrants settled here and in Bensonhurst, Dyker Heights and Gravesend. The beach itself was paved over in the mid-twentieth century to build the Shore Parkway.

sections.heading: Where the beach went
sections.body:
The shoreline that gave the neighborhood its name is gone. It was paved over during the mid-twentieth century to create the Shore Parkway. On the northwestern half a promenade was built to give residents access to a sea wall; the southwestern half was filled in the early 1940s with land excavated during construction of the Shore Parkway, which extended Bensonhurst Park with ballfields and, later, the Caesar's Bay shopping center.

A NYC Parks historical sign in Bath Playground explains where the name came from: the town of Bath in England, founded by the Romans in the first century A.D., whose Roman bath complex was discovered largely intact in 1755.

St. Finbar's parish was founded in 1880 and its present church at 138 Bay 20th Street was dedicated in 1912. Based on the 2020 Census the neighborhood's population was 33,070, about 41 percent Asian American and 40 percent White.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The D is the neighborhood's subway. The 20th Avenue station on the BMT West End Line sits on the border of Bensonhurst and Bath Beach, and only the D stops there. The Bay Parkway station on the same line is recorded in Bensonhurst, Bath Beach and Gravesend; the D calls there at all times, and as of December 2024 one southbound R and two southbound W trains terminate there during the weekday morning rush.

Other nearby West End Line stations belong to their neighbors: 18th Avenue is in Bensonhurst, and 25th Avenue and Bay 50th Street are in Gravesend. No NYC Ferry landing serves Bath Beach.

sections.heading: The 86th Street strip on film
sections.body:
During the 1970s Bath Beach's commercial strip along 86th Street was used for scenes in The French Connection (1971), in the opening credits of Welcome Back, Kotter, and most famously in the opening scene of Saturday Night Fever (1977), in which Tony Manero buys two stacked slices at Lenny's Pizza. Lenny's Pizza, at 1969 86th Street, closed permanently on February 19, 2023 after some seventy years, so the pizzeria is no longer there to visit. The strip was used again in 2016 for the filming of the Red Hot Chili Peppers video for Go Robot.

Samurai Sushi, at 1709 86th Street, is near the Bath Avenue end of that strip. More places to eat stand on Bath Avenue itself: La Chapincita at 1806, Cairo RX Cafe at 1932 and Gyro Mania at 2151.

faq.question: How do I get to Bath Beach?
faq.answer: By D train. The 20th Avenue station on the BMT West End Line sits on the border of Bensonhurst and Bath Beach, and the Bay Parkway station on the same line is recorded in Bensonhurst, Bath Beach and Gravesend. The neighboring West End stations belong elsewhere: 18th Avenue is in Bensonhurst, and 25th Avenue and Bay 50th Street are in Gravesend.

faq.question: Is there still a beach at Bath Beach?
faq.answer: No. The beach was paved over during the mid-twentieth century to create the Shore Parkway. A promenade on the northwestern half gives access to a sea wall, and the southwestern half was filled in the early 1940s with material excavated for the parkway.

faq.question: Can I still get a slice at Lenny's Pizza?
faq.answer: No. The pizzeria from the opening scene of Saturday Night Fever, at 1969 86th Street, closed permanently on February 19, 2023 after some seventy years in business.

faq.question: Why is it called Bath Beach?
faq.answer: After the English spa town of Bath, in Somerset. A NYC Parks historical sign in Bath Playground sets out the connection, back to the Roman town founded in the first century A.D.

faq.question: Which parks are in Bath Beach?
faq.answer: Bath Beach Park on the Shore Parkway, Bath Playground on Bath Avenue, and Bensonhurst Park on Cropsey Avenue, which NYC Parks describes as serving both the Bensonhurst and Bath Beach neighborhoods. The Shore Parkway Greenway runs along the waterfront and is reachable from Bensonhurst Park's Bay Parkway side.

faq.question: Where can I eat in Bath Beach?
faq.answer: On Bath Avenue: La Chapincita at 1806, Cairo RX Cafe at 1932 and Gyro Mania at 2151. Samurai Sushi is at 1709 86th Street, near the Bath Avenue end of that strip.

places.name: Bensonhurst Park
places.address: Cropsey Avenue between 21st Avenue and Bay Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11214
places.summary: About 17.5 acres on the Brooklyn waterfront, which NYC Parks describes as serving both the Bensonhurst and Bath Beach neighborhoods. It has a central lawn, basketball and handball courts, baseball and softball fields, a children's playground, eight hard-court tennis courts and access to the Shore Parkway Greenway.
places.history: Advocacy for a park here began in 1891 and the city acquired the first land in 1895, with additions in 1924 and 1944; the 1940s extension used land excavated during construction of the Shore (Belt) Parkway. A $6.5 million renovation announced in 2016 ran from September 2019 to 2021.

places.name: Bath Playground
places.address: Bath Avenue between 24th Avenue and Bay 37th Street, Brooklyn, NY 11214
places.summary: A 1.16-acre playground with basketball, bocce, handball and soccer facilities and spray showers. It carries the NYC Parks historical sign that explains the neighborhood's name and its origin in Bath, England.

places.name: Bath Beach Park
places.address: Shore Parkway between Bay 14th Street and Bay 16th Street, Brooklyn, NY 11214
places.summary: Nearly three acres named for the neighborhood around it, with a children's play area, chess tables, cast-iron water fountains and an oceanic-themed spray shower. NYC Parks opened $5.4 million of renovations to the playground.

places.name: Ulmer Park Library
places.address: 2602 Bath Avenue at 26th Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11214
places.summary: A Brooklyn Public Library branch, in its current building since 1963. It holds a large Russian and Chinese book collection, and it was the first BPL branch to implement computer-networked circulation, in 1988.
places.history: The branch opened as a sub-library in 1951 and grew into a full library within five years. It was renovated in 2016 with a new roof, furniture, LED lighting and a new floor.

places.name: Shore Parkway Greenway
places.address: Along the Shore Parkway shorefront, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A waterfront bike path and promenade built on the former Bath Beach shoreline after it was paved over for the Shore Parkway, giving pedestrians and cyclists a route along the sea wall. It is reachable from Bensonhurst Park's Bay Parkway side.

places.name: Bay Parkway Station (Dual System BRT)
places.address: Elevated above Bay Parkway at 86th Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A working D-train station on the BMT West End Line, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on July 6, 2005 under reference number 05000670 as part of the New York City Subway System submission. Its locale is recorded as Bensonhurst, Bath Beach and Gravesend.
places.history: The elevated station opened on July 29, 1916. The line beneath it began as a surface excursion railway to Coney Island, the Brooklyn, Bath and Coney Island Railroad, established in 1862.

places.name: St. Finbar Roman Catholic Church
places.summary: A parish founded in 1880 whose present church building was dedicated in 1912.

places.name: Anthony Catanzaro Square
places.address: Traffic triangle at West 16th Street, Avenue Y and Bay 50th Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A small Greenstreets memorial triangle that the New York City Council designated in 1963 to honor Private First Class Anthony Catanzaro, 1916 to 1943, killed in the Second World War.
places.history: Catanzaro's ship was torpedoed on November 26, 1943 en route to the Italian front, and he was posthumously awarded the Purple Heart. His younger brother Joseph, who survived the June 6, 1944 landings in Normandy, had a flagpole installed and shrubs planted here.
